Spain's names come from three layers stacked on each other: pre-Roman
peoples (Cantabri, Astures, Vascones, Galli), Latin (Castilla's castles,
Extremadura's frontier), and Arabic (Andalucía, the Guadal- rivers -
wadi al-, 'river of'). Naming which layer a name belongs to is usually
Ids drop the tildes, so Cataluña is 'cataluna'.
asturias: Named for the Astures, a people Rome needed two hundred years to subdue; the name may come from a river, the Astura.
The only part of Iberia the Moors never held, which is why every later Spanish king's heir is called the Prince of Asturias.
cantabria: From the Cantabri, the other people who held out against Rome — Augustus came in person to finish the war, and it still took a decade.
The Altamira caves here hold paintings 36,000 years old; when they were found in 1880 nobody believed they were prehistoric.
pais-vasco: "Basque country" — Vasco is from the Vascones, the Roman name for the people. They call it Euskadi, from their own word for their language.
Basque is unrelated to any other living language on earth, and was spoken here before Indo-European reached Europe.
galicia: From the Callaeci or Gallaeci, the tribes Rome met in the north-west — the same root, distantly, as Gaul and Wales: a word outsiders used for Celts.
Santiago de Compostela is here, the end of the pilgrim road, and Galician is close enough to Portuguese that the two were one language until the 1300s.
navarra: Probably Basque nava, a flat valley among hills, plus -erri, land.
An independent kingdom for seven centuries, straddling the Pyrenees; France kept the northern half until 1620.
la-rioja: The river Oja, or possibly rio oja from the Arabic — and the article stays: it is La Rioja, never just Rioja, for the region.
Spain's smallest mainland region, and the one whose name is on more bottles than any other.
cataluna: Nobody is certain: most likely from the castlà, the castellans who held the frontier castles, or from Gothia plus Alania.
Barcelona was the Frankish empire's southern march against the Moors, which is why the region faces the Mediterranean and France more than Madrid.
castilla-y-leon: Castilla is "land of castles", the frontier forts against the Moors; León is not the lion but Latin legio, the Seventh Legion's camp.
The lion on its arms is a pun the heralds could not resist — the city was a legion, not a cat.
aragon: Named for the river Aragón, which itself is probably pre-Roman and pre-Basque.
Its marriage to Castilla in 1469 made Spain, and its own empire had already taken Sicily, Sardinia and Naples.
madrid: From Arabic al-Majrit, "source of water" — the Moorish fortress was named for its streams, and the Christians kept the name.
A provincial town until Philip II moved the court here in 1561, chosen largely for sitting in the middle of the country.
castilla-la-mancha: Castilla again, plus La Mancha, from Arabic al-mansha, "the dry land" — and it is: a high, flat, hot plain.
Don Quixote rode here, and the windmills he charged still stand on the ridge at Consuegra.
islas-baleares: From Greek ballein, "to throw" — the islanders were slingers, and Carthage and Rome both hired them.
Mallorca and Menorca are simply the larger and the smaller, from Latin maior and minor.
comunidad-valenciana: Valencia is Latin valentia, "strength" or "valour" — a name Rome gave several towns, and this one kept.
Its Albufera lagoon is where paella comes from, cooked over orange wood with rabbit and beans rather than seafood.
extremadura: Not "extremely hard": it is extrema durii, the land beyond the Duero — the outer edge of the reconquered frontier.
Cortés, Pizarro and Balboa all came from this one poor province, which is why so many places in the Americas carry Extremaduran names.
murcia: Uncertain: possibly Latin myrtea, the myrtle, or murtia from the Arabic Mursiyah — the Moors founded the city in 825.
Its huerta is irrigated by canals the Moors dug eleven centuries ago, still running on the same gradients.
andalucia: From Arabic al-Andalus, the Moorish name for all of Iberia — which may itself come from the Vandals who passed through.
The Moors held it for nearly eight hundred years, until 1492: longer than the time since, and the Alhambra, the Mezquita and flamenco all carry it.
